## Yes – you can serve map tiles from **GitHub Pages** with **zero backend** and use them in a MapLibre GL JS map.  
The trick is to put the tiles in a format that works with a pure‑static host (no “/z/x/y.png” routing required) and make sure the browser can request the bytes it needs.  

The most robust way today is to use **PMTiles** – a single‑file archive that stores vector or raster tiles and is read by the client via HTTP **Range** requests.  
GitHub Pages (or any static‑file host) serves those range requests out‑of‑the‑box, so you get a full tile server without any server‑side code.

Below is a complete, step‑by‑step guide:

---

## 1. Choose the tile format

| Option | What you get | When it makes sense |
|--------|--------------|---------------------|
| **PMTiles (vector)** | One `.pmtiles` file that contains all vector layers (roads, water, labels, …). | Most use‑cases – you want a single file, easy CDN caching, and you don’t need a custom XYZ folder structure. |
| **PMTiles (raster)** | One `.pmtiles` file that contains PNG/JPEG tiles (satellite, orthophoto). | When you need imagery instead of vector data. |
| **XYZ folder (`/z/x/y.{pbf|png|jpg}`)** | A directory tree of individual tile files. | Works on GitHub Pages too, but you must keep the whole tree in the repo (or in a release) and you lose the “single‑file” convenience of PMTiles. |

**Recommendation:** start with a **vector PMTiles** file. It’s the smallest, easiest to version, and works with the `pmtiles://` protocol that MapLibre provides.

---

## 2. Create a PMTiles file

You can generate PMTiles in many ways; the two most common pipelines are:

### 2‑a. From an existing MBTiles file (easiest if you already have MBTiles)

```bash
# Install the official CLI (single binary, no npm needed)
# macOS / Linux:
curl -L https://github.com/protomaps/go-pmtiles/releases/download/v2.5.0/pmtiles-2.5.0-linux-amd64 -o pmtiles
chmod +x pmtiles

# Convert
./pmtiles convert mytiles.mbtiles mytiles.pmtiles
```

### 2‑b. Directly from source data with tippecanoe (v2.17+)

```bash
# tippecanoe can output PMTiles directly
tippecanoe -zg -o mytiles.pmtiles mydata.geojson
```

> **Tip:** If you need a global OSM‑based basemap, you can download a ready‑made PMTiles from **Protomaps** (e.g. `https://github.com/protomaps/basemaps/releases`). Remember the required OSM attribution.

### 2‑c. From OSM with Planetiler (for larger or custom schemas)

```bash
java -jar planetiler.jar --area=monaco --output=monaco.pmtiles
```

> **Result:** a single `*.pmtiles` file, typically a few megabytes for a city‑scale dataset, up to a few hundred megabytes for a country.

---

## 3. Check the file size limits on GitHub Pages

| Hosting method | Max file size (per file) |
|----------------|--------------------------|
| **GitHub repository (committed files)** | 100 MiB (GitHub will reject larger files). |
| **GitHub Releases (assets)** | 2 GiB per asset (served from `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/download/...`). |
| **GitHub Pages (built from the repo)** | Same 100 MiB limit because the file becomes part of the repo. |
| **GitHub Pages with a *release* asset** | You can reference the release URL directly; the file is **not** part of the site build, so the 100 MiB limit does not apply. |

**What to do:**  

*If your PMTiles file is ≤ 100 MiB* – just add it to the repo (e.g. `public/tiles/world.pmtiles`) and push.  

*If it’s larger* – upload it as a **release asset** and use the raw release URL (`https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/download/v1.0.0/world.pmtiles`). The release URL works with range requests just like a normal static file.

---

## 4. Make the file publicly reachable with CORS

GitHub Pages (and GitHub release assets) already send the required CORS headers:

```
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Accept-Ranges: bytes
```

So you **do not need any extra configuration**. Just verify in the browser dev‑tools that a `Range` request to the URL returns `206 Partial Content`.

---

## 5. Add the PMTiles protocol to your MapLibre map

### 5‑a. Install the `pmtiles` library

```bash
npm install pmtiles maplibre-gl
# or, if you use Yarn / pnpm
```

### 5‑b. Register the protocol **once** (e.g. in your app’s entry point)

```js
// src/pmtiles-setup.js
import * as pmtiles from 'pmtiles';
import maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl';

// Create a singleton protocol instance
const protocol = new pmtiles.Protocol();

// Register the custom scheme with MapLibre
maplibregl.addProtocol('pmtiles', protocol.tile);

// Export the protocol in case you need to clean up later
export default protocol;
```

> **Why register once?** The protocol maintains an internal cache of the archive’s header. Registering it repeatedly (e.g. inside a React component’s `useEffect`) can cause duplicate fetches and memory leaks.

### 5‑c. Use the PMTiles URL in a style

```js
// src/map.js
import maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl';
import './pmtiles-setup'; // ensures the protocol is registered

// Choose the URL based on where you stored the file
const pmtilesUrl = 'pmtiles://https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/tiles/world.pmtiles';
// If you used a release asset:
// const pmtilesUrl = 'pmtiles://https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/download/v1.0.0/world.pmtiles';

const map = new maplibregl.Map({
  container: 'map',
  style: {
    version: 8,
    sources: {
      // One source points at the whole PMTiles archive
      world: {
        type: 'vector',
        url: pmtilesUrl
      }
    },
    layers: [
      // Example: water polygons
      {
        id: 'water',
        type: 'fill',
        source: 'world',
        'source-layer': 'water',
        paint: { 'fill-color': '#a0c8f0' }
      },
      // Example: road lines
      {
        id: 'roads',
        type: 'line',
        source: 'world',
        'source-layer': 'road',
        paint: {
          'line-color': '#777',
          'line-width': ['interpolate', ['linear'], ['zoom'], 5, 0.5, 15, 4]
        }
      },
      // Add as many layers as you need – each just points to the same source
    ]
  },
  center: [0, 0],
  zoom: 2
});
```

**Key points in the style:**

* `type: 'vector'` (or `'raster'` / `'raster-dem'` if you have those).
* `url: 'pmtiles://https://…/mytiles.pmtiles'` – **never** use a `tiles:` array for PMTiles. The protocol reads the archive header and automatically supplies `minzoom`, `maxzoom`, and the TileJSON that MapLibre expects.
* Each layer uses `source: 'world'` and a `source-layer` that matches the layer name inside the PMTiles file (you can see those names with `pmtiles show world.pmtiles`).

### 5‑d. (Optional) Add a terrain source

If you have a raster‑DEM PMTiles (e.g. Terrarium‑encoded elevation), add it like this:

```json
"terrain": {
  "source": "elevation",
  "type": "raster-dem",
  "url": "pmtiles://https://…/elevation.pmtiles",
  "encoding": "terrarium"
}
```

Then enable terrain on the map:

```js
map.setTerrain({ source: 'elevation', exaggeration: 1.5 });
```

---

## 6. Deploy to GitHub Pages

1. **Add the PMTiles file** (or keep it as a release asset).  
2. Commit your `index.html`, JS bundle, CSS, etc. to the `gh-pages` branch (or to the `docs/` folder on the default branch if you use the “GitHub Pages from /docs” option).  
3. Push. GitHub will build the site and serve it at `https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/`.

If you used a **release asset**, you don’t need to push the large file; just make sure the URL in your code points to the release asset.

### Example repo layout

```
my-map/
├─ .gitignore
├─ index.html          ← loads the bundled JS
├─ src/
│   ├─ map.js
│   └─ pmtiles-setup.js
├─ public/
│   └─ tiles/
│       └─ world.pmtiles   ← only if ≤100 MiB
├─ package.json
└─ README.md
```

Deploy command (using `gh-pages` npm package, or any CI you prefer):

```bash
npm run build               # creates dist/
npx gh-pages -d dist        # pushes to gh-pages branch
```

---

## 7. Verify everything works

1. Open the site in a browser.  
2. Open DevTools → Network.  
3. Look for a request like:

```
GET https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/tiles/world.pmtiles
Range: bytes=0-1023
```

You should see a **206 Partial Content** response. Subsequent tile requests will be similar, each fetching only the byte range for the needed tile.

If you see **404** or **CORS** errors, double‑check:

* The URL is correct (no extra `?raw=1` needed for GitHub Pages).  
* The file is publicly readable (release assets are always public).  
* The server returns `Accept-Ranges: bytes` (GitHub does).  

---

## 8. What if you prefer the classic XYZ folder layout?

GitHub Pages can also serve a static tile tree:

```
/tiles/12/3456/7890.pbf
```

**Pros:** works with any MapLibre source (`type: 'vector'`, `tiles: ['https://…/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf']`).  

**Cons:**  

* You must keep the whole folder in the repo (or in a release asset and copy it into the site at build time).  
* No automatic min/max‑zoom metadata – you have to set `minzoom`/`maxzoom` yourself.  
* Large numbers of files can make the repo heavy and slow to clone.

If you go this route, the MapLibre source looks like:

```json
{
  "type": "vector",
  "tiles": ["https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf"],
  "minzoom": 0,
  "maxzoom": 14
}
```

Everything else (CORS, range requests) works the same because each tile is a separate static file.

Below is a **step‑by‑step checklist** you can run locally to:

1. **Make sure the archive is not corrupted** (`pmtiles verify`).
2. **Read the header / TileJSON** – you’ll see the min/max zoom, bounds, and for vector archives the list of *source‑layers* (the layer names you’ll use in a MapLibre style).
3. **Optionally peek at a real tile** and decode it so you can double‑check the exact layer names and feature schema.
4. **(Optional) Export a tiny subset** to test‑upload quickly.

All of this can be done with the **official `pmtiles` CLI** (no Node runtime needed) **or** with a tiny Node script that uses the same library the browser uses.

---

## 1️⃣ Install the PMTiles CLI (once)

| OS | Command |
|----|---------|
| macOS (brew) | `brew install protomaps/tap/pmtiles` |
| Linux (deb) | `wget https://github.com/protomaps/go-pmtiles/releases/download/v2.5.0/pmtiles-linux-amd64 && chmod +x pmtiles-linux-amd64 && sudo mv pmtiles-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/pmtiles` |
| Windows (scoop) | `scoop bucket add protomaps https://github.com/protomaps/scoop-bucket && scoop install pmtiles` |
| Any platform (binary) | <https://github.com/protomaps/go-pmtiles/releases> – download the appropriate `pmtiles-<os>-<arch>` and put it on your `$PATH`. |

> **Tip:** The binary is a single ~5 MB file, no Node, Python or Java required.

---

## 2️⃣ Verify the archive is structurally sound

```bash
pmtiles verify mydata.pmtiles
```

*What you’ll see*

```
✔︎  Header checksum OK
✔︎  Tile index checksum OK
✔︎  Tile data checksum OK
✔︎  No overlapping tile entries
✔︎  File size matches header
```

If any check fails the CLI will exit with a non‑zero status and print the problem (e.g. “Tile offset out of range”). In that case you need to rebuild the archive (or run `pmtiles extract` to salvage a good subset).

---

## 3️⃣ Show the header / TileJSON (layers, zoom range, bounds)

```bash
pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles
```

Typical output for a **vector** archive:

```
File: mydata.pmtiles
Version: 2
Tile type: vector
Bounds: -180.0,-85.0511,180.0,85.0511
Zoom range: 0‑14
Tile count: 1 234 567
Metadata (JSON):
{
  "name": "My custom basemap",
  "description": "OpenStreetMap‑derived vector tiles",
  "attribution": "© OpenStreetMap contributors",
  "vector_layers": [
    {"id":"water","description":"Water bodies"},
    {"id":"landuse","description":"Land use polygons"},
    {"id":"roads","description":"Road network"},
    {"id":"places","description":"Cities, towns, villages"},
    {"id":"building","description":"Buildings"}
  ]
}
```

*Key fields*

| Field | Why it matters |
|-------|----------------|
| `Tile type` | `vector`, `raster` or `raster-dem`. Determines which `type:` you put in the MapLibre style. |
| `Zoom range` | `minzoom` / `maxzoom` that MapLibre will read automatically when you use `url:` (not `tiles:`). |
| `vector_layers` (or `raster_layers`) | The exact **`source-layer`** names you will reference in your style. |
| `Metadata` | Anything you passed via `--metadata` when you built the file (e.g. `attribution`, `name`). MapLibre does not read it automatically, but you can expose it in your UI. |

If the file is **raster** you’ll see something like:

```
Tile type: raster
Raster format: png
Raster layers: ["satellite"]
```

For a **raster‑dem** you’ll see `Raster format: png` plus `"encoding":"terrarium"` if you set it during creation.

---

## 4️⃣ Peek at a real tile (optional but handy)

Sometimes you want to be 100 % sure the layer names inside a tile match the header, or you want to inspect the feature schema. The CLI can dump a tile, and a short Node script can decode it.

### 4.1 Dump a raw tile with the CLI

```bash
# Grab tile z=5, x=10, y=12 (any tile that exists)
pmtiles get mydata.pmtiles 5/10/12 > tile.pbf
# Show its size
ls -lh tile.pbf
```

If the file is empty (`0 B`) you probably asked for a tile outside the archive’s coverage.

### 4.2 Decode the tile locally (Node)

```bash
# 1️⃣ Install the tiny helpers (once)
npm i pmtiles @mapbox/vector-tile pbf

# 2️⃣ Create a script: inspect-tile.js
cat > inspect-tile.js <<'EOF'
import { PMTiles } from "pmtiles";
import { VectorTile } from "@mapbox/vector-tile";
import Protobuf from "pbf";
import fs from "fs";
import path from "path";

const [,, archivePath, z, x, y] = process.argv;
if (!archivePath || !z || !x || !y) {
  console.error("Usage: node inspect-tile.js <archive.pmtiles> <z> <x> <y>");
  process.exit(1);
}

// Open the archive (local file)
const source = new PMTiles(archivePath);
await source.open();

// Get the raw tile bytes
const tile = await source.getTile(z, x, y);
if (!tile) {
  console.error("Tile not found in the archive");
  process.exit(1);
}

// Decode the vector tile
const vt = new VectorTile(new Protobuf(tile));
console.log(`Tile ${z}/${x}/${y} contains ${Object.keys(vt.layers).length} layers:`);

for (const [layerName, layer] of Object.entries(vt.layers)) {
  console.log(`- ${layerName}: ${layer.length} features`);
  // Show a sample feature (first one) if you want
  const feature = layer.feature(0);
  if (feature) {
    console.log(`  sample feature properties:`, feature.properties);
  }
}
EOF

# 3️⃣ Run it
node inspect-tile.js mydata.pmtiles 5 10 12
```

**What you’ll see**

```
Tile 5/10/12 contains 5 layers:
- water: 23 features
- landuse: 87 features
- roads: 154 features
- places: 12 features
- building: 321 features
```

That list **must match** the `vector_layers` array you saw in `pmtiles show`. If you see extra or missing layers, you probably built the archive with a different schema than you expect.

> **Why use a script?**  
> * The CLI can only show the header; it does **not** decode the tile contents.  
> * Decoding lets you verify that the geometry type (point/line/polygon) and attribute names are what your style expects.  
> * You can run this script on a single tile (or a loop over a few zoom levels) without uploading anything.

---

## 5️⃣ Quick “preview” without uploading – serve locally

If you want to see the whole style in a browser before you push the file to S3, you can spin up a tiny static server that serves the `.pmtiles` file with proper CORS and Range headers.

```bash
# Install a tiny static server that supports range requests (http-server)
npm i -g http-server

# Put the file in a folder, e.g. ./public/
mkdir -p public && cp mydata.pmtiles public/

# Serve it (CORS enabled)
http-server public -p 8080 --cors
```

Now in your MapLibre page use:

```js
import * as pmtiles from "pmtiles";
import maplibregl from "maplibre-gl";

const protocol = new pmtiles.Protocol();
maplibregl.addProtocol("pmtiles", protocol.tile);

new maplibregl.Map({
  container: "map",
  style: {
    version: 8,
    sources: {
      mytiles: {
        type: "vector",
        url: "pmtiles://http://localhost:8080/mydata.pmtiles"
      }
    },
    layers: [
      { id: "water", type: "fill", source: "mytiles", "source-layer": "water", paint: { "fill-color": "#a0c8f0" } },
      // …other layers using the same source
    ]
  },
  center: [0, 0],
  zoom: 2
});
```

If the map renders correctly, you’ve verified:

* The file is reachable via range requests.
* The `source-layer` names are correct.
* The zoom range works (over‑zooming will be handled automatically).

When you’re happy, just upload the same `.pmtiles` file to S3/R2/GitHub Pages and keep the same URL in the style.

---

## 6️⃣ (Optional) Extract a tiny test slice

If your archive is huge (hundreds of MB) and you want to upload a **small test file** first, the CLI can cut out a bounding box or a zoom range:

```bash
# Extract only zoom levels 0‑5 (good for quick sanity checks)
pmtiles extract mydata.pmtiles test-small.pmtiles --minzoom 0 --maxzoom 5

# Or extract a geographic window (e.g. Europe)
pmtiles extract mydata.pmtiles test-europe.pmtiles --bbox -10,35,30,60
```

Run the same `pmtiles show` / `verify` on the extracted file – it should be a fraction of the original size but still contain the same layer names.

## 📋 TL;DR Cheat‑Sheet

| Goal | Command | What you get |
|------|---------|--------------|
| **Check integrity** | `pmtiles verify mydata.pmtiles` | Pass/Fail + error details |
| **List layers, zoom range, bounds** | `pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles` | Header + `vector_layers` array |
| **Dump a raw tile** | `pmtiles get mydata.pmtiles 5/10/12 > tile.pbf` | Raw protobuf (size check) |
| **Decode a tile & list feature counts** | Node script (see above) | Exact `source-layer` names & sample properties |
| **Serve locally for a quick MapLibre preview** | `http-server ./public -p 8080 --cors` | Browser can request `pmtiles://http://localhost:8080/...` |
| **Make a tiny test file** | `pmtiles extract … --minzoom 0 --maxzoom 5` | Small PMTiles you can upload first |

### 🎯 What to do next

1. **Run `pmtiles verify`** – if it fails, rebuild the archive.
2. **Run `pmtiles show`** – copy the `vector_layers` (or `raster_layers`) array into your MapLibre style’s `source-layer` fields.
3. **(Optional) Run the Node decoder** on a few tiles to confirm attribute names.
4. **Upload the file** to your static host (S3, R2, GitHub Pages, etc.) **with**:
   * `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000`
   * `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain)
   * `Accept-Ranges: bytes` (most static hosts already send this)
5. **Update the style** to use `url: "pmtiles://https://<your‑host>/<file>.pmtiles"` and test in the browser.

That’s it—your PMTiles archive is now validated, you know exactly which layer names to use, and you can safely push it to production with confidence. Happy mapping! 🚀

No knowledge of the PMTiles file itself. | The PMTiles protocol intercepts the `pmtiles://` URL, opens the file, reads its **header** (bounds, minzoom, maxzoom, tile count, etc.) and returns a **generated TileJSON** that contains the correct `minzoom`/`maxzoom`. | | **Zoom range** | If you don’t also set `minzoom`/`maxzoom` in the source definition, MapLibre defaults to `minzoom: 0`, `maxzoom: 22`. | The values from the header are used automatically. | | **Tile request** | When you zoom beyond the archive’s max (e.g. archive stops at 14, you go to 15+), MapLibre still builds URLs like `…/15/…/…` and sends a range request for those bytes. The PMTiles file has no entry → the protocol returns an empty tile. | MapLibre sees that the source’s `maxzoom` is 14, so for zoom 15 it **over‑zooms**: it asks for the same tile at zoom 14 (or the nearest‑available lower zoom) and the protocol returns that tile. No blank tiles. | | **Result** | Blank tiles (or “no data”) once you exceed the archive’s max zoom. | Correct tiles (or graceful over‑zoom) all the way up to the max you defined. | ### Why the header matters A PMTiles file stores its own metadata in the first few kilobytes: ```text { "version": 1, "bounds": [-180,-85,180,85], "minzoom": 0, "maxzoom": 14, "center": [0,0,2], "tileCount": 123456, … } ``` The **PMTiles protocol** (`pmtiles.Protocol().tile`) reads that block, builds a TileJSON object, and hands it to MapLibre. That TileJSON tells MapLibre exactly which zoom levels exist, so the library can: * stop requesting zoom levels that don’t exist, * automatically over‑zoom (reuse the highest‑available tiles), * correctly compute the source’s `bounds` for `fitBounds`, etc. When you bypass the protocol by using a `tiles:` template, MapLibre never sees that metadata. --- ## How to fix it ### 1. Use the `url` property (recommended) ```json { "type": "vector", "url": "pmtiles://https://my-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/world.pmtiles" } ``` or, if you prefer an HTTPS URL without the `pmtiles://` prefix, register the protocol once and then use a plain URL: ```js import * as pmtiles from 'pmtiles'; import * as maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl'; // Register the protocol globally (do this once, e.g. at app start) const protocol = new pmtiles.Protocol(); maplibregl.addProtocol('pmtiles', protocol.tile); // Now you can use a plain HTTPS URL: const style = { version: 8, sources: { world: { type: 'vector', url: 'https://my-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/world.pmtiles' // <-- no tiles array } }, layers: [ /* … */ ] }; ``` **Result:** MapLibre receives the correct `minzoom`/`maxzoom` from the file and will never request tiles that don’t exist. ### 2. If you *must* use a `tiles:` array (rare) You can still make it work, but you have to **manually supply the zoom limits** so MapLibre knows when to stop requesting higher zooms: ```json { "type": "vector", "tiles": ["pmtiles://https://my-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/world.pmtiles/{z}/{x}/{y}"], "minzoom": 0, "maxzoom": 14 // <-- must match the archive’s maxzoom } ``` *Pros*: Works with older code that expects a `tiles` array. *Cons*: You have to keep the numbers in sync with the archive; if you regenerate the PMTiles with a different zoom range you’ll have to update the style manually. ### 3. Verify the archive’s zoom range Run the CLI to be sure: ```bash pmtiles show world.pmtiles # Look for "minzoom" and "maxzoom" in the output ``` If the CLI reports `maxzoom: 14` but your style’s `maxzoom` is 22 (or omitted), you’ve found the mismatch. ### 4. Double‑check that the protocol is registered **before** the map is created If you add the protocol after the `new maplibregl.Map()` call, the first source creation may already have used the default TileJSON (no header). Register it early: ```js // In a React app, put this in the top‑level component or a separate init file import * as pmtiles from 'pmtiles'; import * as maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl'; const protocol = new pmtiles.Protocol(); maplibregl.addProtocol('pmtiles', protocol.tile); ``` --- ## Quick checklist for “blank tiles after a certain zoom” | ✅ | Check | |---|-------| | **Protocol registration** | `maplibregl.addProtocol('pmtiles', …)` runs before any `new maplibregl.Map()` | | **Source definition** | Uses `url: 'pmtiles://…'` (or plain HTTPS URL after registration) **not** `tiles: [...]` | | **Zoom limits** | If you *must* use `tiles:`, you have `minzoom`/`maxzoom` set to the same values reported by `pmtiles show`. | | **CORS & Range support** | Host returns `Access‑Control‑Allow‑Origin: *` (or your domain) and `Accept‑Ranges: bytes`. | | **File integrity** | `pmtiles verify world.pmtiles` reports no errors. | | **Cache headers** | Long `Cache‑Control` (e.g. `public, max-age=31536000`) so the CDN can cache range responses. | If all of the above are true and you still see blanks, open the browser dev‑tools → **Network** tab, filter for the PMTiles URL, and look at the request that fails: * **Status 206 (Partial Content)** – good, the range request succeeded. * **Status 200 (Full file)** – the server is ignoring the `Range` header (common on some static hosts). Fix by switching to a host that supports range requests (S3, Cloudflare R2, Netlify, Vercel, etc.). * **Status 404** – the URL template is wrong (e.g., extra `/` or missing `{z}` placeholder). --- ## Example: Full working snippet (vanilla JS) ```html PMTiles with MapLibre
